title: Real‑World Text Processing Combos 🔗
description: Chain sed and awk in pipelines to solve complex log analysis, CSV manipulation, and reporting.

slides.title: The Unix Philosophy in Action 🧠
slides.content:
## Do One Thing Well, Compose

`sed` excels at line‑oriented transformations (substitutions, deleting, inserting). `awk` excels at field‑based calculations and reporting. Together they form an unstoppable duo.

A typical pipeline: `grep` to filter, `sed` to clean, `awk` to compute.

slides.title: Clean CSV with sed, Summarise with awk
slides.content: Remove empty lines and comments, then compute average of column 3:
slides.codeSnippet: sed '/^#/d;/^$/d' data.csv | awk -F, '{ sum+=$3; count++ } END { print sum/count }'

quizData.question: Why would you use `sed` before `awk` in a pipeline?

options.text: To clean or pre‑format text before field‑based processing

quizData.explanation: sed can strip unwanted lines, replace delimiters, or fix formatting so awk receives clean input.

slides.title: Apache Log Analysis Example 🌐
slides.content:
## Extract Top 10 IPs by Requests

Given an Apache combined log, we can:
1. `sed` to remove lines that are not access entries (if any).
2. `awk` to extract the first field (IP).
3. `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head`.

But we can also use `awk` associative arrays to count and sort itself (though sorting requires `asort` in GNU awk). We'll combine classic tools.

slides.title: Top IPs Pipeline
slides.content: Count IP addresses from an access log:
slides.codeSnippet: awk '{ print $1 }' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10

quizData.question: awk can completely replace the `sort | uniq -c` pattern for counting.
quizData.explanation: awk can accumulate counts in an associative array and then output them, eliminating the need for sort/uniq in the pipeline.

slides.title: Reformatting Reports with awk 📊
slides.content:
## From Raw Data to Readable Tables

Using `printf` and `BEGIN`/`END`, awk can produce formatted reports.

Example: display disk usage as a table:
```bash
df -h | awk 'NR>1 { printf "%-20s %5s\n", $1, $5 }'
```

slides.title: sed + awk: A Complex Example 🧪
slides.content:
## Transform and Calculate

Problem: Convert a log with timestamps like `[2026-05-22 10:15:01]` into a CSV of date and count of events per day.

Pipeline:
```bash
grep 'ERROR' app.log | sed 's/\[/,/; s/\]//' | awk -F',' '{ print $2 }' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c
```
But we can also use awk with match() to extract date and count.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: When chaining sed and awk, test each stage separately: `command1 | head`, then add `| command2 | head`, etc. Build incrementally.
